title: Pre-operational inspection and sanitation records
audience: Cleaners and team leads who complete inspection checklists and sanitation records before production.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish a completed cleaning checklist from environmental monitoring, ATP swabs, microbiological sampling and official production release.
Compare observed conditions with the operator's sign-off checklist without certifying production readiness.
Record unverified tasks clearly, and refuse to sign off a premature restart.

instruction.heading: What a checklist can and cannot show
instruction.body: A completed cleaning checklist is a record that the listed cleaning steps were carried out and that someone says so. It is useful evidence of work done, and it is one part of the food safety program. It does not prove that micro-organisms are absent, and it does not prove that a line is ready to run. Those are different questions with different evidence. The Safe Food Australia guide to the standards describes cleanliness and the cleaning and sanitising of equipment as separate matters under Standard 3.2.2 (clauses 19 and 20, located from the guide's contents; the clause wording was not read for this draft). The guide also quotes the definition of 'clean' in Standard 3.1.1 as a physical test: the surface is clean to touch and free of visible extraneous matter. A surface can pass that physical test and still need verification by other means. Keep the cleaning record, the verification results, the monitoring results and the release decision in separate places in your head and in the record.

instruction.heading: Verification tools and what their results mean
instruction.body: Several tools are used to check cleaning, and each answers a narrower question than the checklist. The NSW Food Authority guide on environmental swabbing (undated, reference FI170/1303) describes swabs as a way to verify cleaning and sanitation, and notes that counts from swabs, contact plates and dipslides are semi-quantitative. Single results are of limited value; trends over time are more useful. ATP tests detect residue on a surface and give fast feedback, which suits a pre-start check, but the same guide says results are site-specific and are best read as a trend. Contact plates and dipslides are not conclusive for detecting specific pathogens such as Salmonella or Listeria. The guide also advises waiting for the sanitiser's contact time to pass before sampling, commonly five to fifteen minutes, which is a useful example of why timing must be recorded. Importantly, the guide presents sampling as verification and monitoring. It does not say that a test result replaces cleaning or that it is a production release. Your role is to carry out the steps you are assigned, record them, and make sure the right test is done at the right time by the person authorised to do it.

instruction.heading: Comparing observed conditions
instruction.body: Before a shift starts, compare what you can see with the operator's sign-off checklist. Look at each item and ask whether you have observed it yourself. Where you have seen a step done, record what you saw. Where you have not seen it, or cannot see the area, mark it as not verified. Do not tick a step that you have not observed, and do not carry a tick forward from a previous shift. Be specific about the zone, the time and the method. If a checklist line covers a large item, such as a whole conveyor, note which sections you checked and which you did not reach, for example the underside of a belt. A cleaner's sign-off covers the cleaning and observations that the cleaner made. It is not a release of the line, and it is not a certification that the line is free of hazards. If the checklist asks for a judgement you are not competent to make, record the observation and pass the judgement to the person who is.

instruction.heading: Production release and premature restart
instruction.body: Production release is a separate decision made by the authorised person under the site's food safety program. It depends on the completed cleaning record, the verification and monitoring results that the program requires, any maintenance that changed the equipment, and the owner's written decision. A line may be restarted only after that decision has been made. A premature restart is one where production resumes while some of those inputs are missing or unresolved. Treat any request to restart early as a stop-work trigger. Where a restart follows maintenance, the earlier sign-off no longer describes the equipment, which is why the plant-state checks in the related degreasing material matter here too. A supervisor's pressure, a customer's deadline or a visual impression that the line looks clean does not change the release process. None of these is a substitute for the test results or the authorised decision.

instruction.heading: Refusing a premature restart
instruction.body: If someone asks you to sign that a line is ready to restart while tests, monitoring or release decisions are still pending, refuse to sign. Explain plainly what is pending. You might say that the cleaning is recorded, that the results are not back, and that you cannot sign for release. Then record the request, the person who made it, the time, the tasks that are unverified and the person you escalated to. Escalate to the authorised supervisor or food safety owner, and keep the stop in place until they confirm in writing how the matter is resolved. Do not sign a version of the record that describes the line as ready. Do not agree to add a note that cancels the concern. A refusal is a normal and required part of the job, and recording it protects the site, the team and the customers.

instruction.heading: Writing a record that can be checked
instruction.body: A useful sanitation record shows what was done, where, when, by whom, and how it was checked. Write the date, time, zone, the item checked, the observed condition, the method of checking and your initials. Use plain words. Avoid describing the line as sterile, pathogen-free, allergen-free or clear, because you cannot establish those claims from a cleaning checklist. Mark unverified steps and state why. Corrections should be made by striking through the entry with a single line, initialling it and giving the reason and date, rather than rubbing out or rewriting. Keep the record with the other site records, and retain it for the period the site procedure requires. An auditor or the owner should be able to follow each line from the checklist to the observation to the person who recorded it.

procedure: Read the operator's current sign-off checklist and confirm which lines are cleaning steps, which are verification or monitoring, and which are release decisions.
Walk the zone and compare each cleaning line with what you can see, checking hard-to-reach areas where the checklist requires it.
Mark any step you have not seen, or cannot reach, as not verified, and say why.
Do not tick a step that you did not observe, and do not carry forward a tick from an earlier shift.
If a verification test is required, confirm who performs it, when it is due, and that the sanitiser contact time has passed before sampling, as the site procedure states.
If someone asks you to sign for a restart while a test, monitoring result or release decision is pending, refuse, record the request and escalate to the authorised person.
Record unverified tasks, the authorised person who must verify them, and the time you handed the record over.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor asks you to sign that a line is ready to restart. The cleaning is recorded as done, but the swab results from the same morning are still pending. (Example scenario; the times and results are fictional.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you sign, and what do you do next?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not sign for restart. The cleaning record can be signed for the cleaning you observed, but the results are pending and release is a separate decision by the authorised person. Record the request, the supervisor's name, the time and the pending results. Escalate to the food safety owner, and keep the stop in place until the owner decides in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague has ticked 'underside of conveyor sanitised' on the checklist. When you walk the zone, you see sanitiser marks on the top surface, but the underside has no visible wet film and the access panel is still closed. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which entry do you make, and do you change the colleague's tick?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not change or remove the colleague's tick without speaking to them and recording your observation. Mark the underside as not verified, state that the top surface was observed and the underside was not reached, and record the access panel status. Tell the team lead so that the line is not released on that item until the underside is confirmed by the person authorised to do so.

workedExamples.situation: A quick check after cleaning shows a result that the team regards as too high for a section of the line. The team suggests wiping the section again and testing until the result looks better. (Example scenario; the reading is fictional.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is re-wiping and re-testing until the result passes an acceptable response?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. Testing repeatedly until a result looks acceptable is not verification. Record the original reading, the time, the method and the contact time that applied. Any further cleaning or retest should be decided by the food safety owner under the site procedure, and each result should be recorded, including the first one. Refer the matter and keep the section on hold until the owner decides.

equipmentAndPpe: Operator sign-off checklist for the current pre-operational inspection.
Record form with spaces for not-verified items, reasons and the person to verify them.
Torch for checking hard-to-reach surfaces, used within site hygiene rules.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the SDS for any sanitiser used during checks.
Verification kit, such as ATP or swab materials, only if the cleaner has been trained and authorised to use it.
Pen or approved electronic record system, with a way to record corrections and dates.
Site food hygiene clothing, hair restraint and jewellery controls, as the site requires.

commonErrors.error: Treating a completed cleaning checklist as proof that micro-organisms are absent.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep cleaning records separate from verification, monitoring and release, and say which one a record supports.

commonErrors.error: Ticking a step that was not seen, or carrying a tick forward from a previous shift.
commonErrors.prevention: Observe each step, and record anything unseen with the reason.

commonErrors.error: Re-wiping and re-testing until a result looks acceptable.
commonErrors.prevention: Record every result and refer repeat testing to the food safety owner under the site procedure.

commonErrors.error: Signing for a restart under time pressure.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse, record the request and escalate; keep the stop in place until the owner decides in writing.

commonErrors.error: Describing the line as sterile, pathogen-free or allergen-free.
commonErrors.prevention: Use factual wording about the cleaning done and the observations made.

commonErrors.error: Rewriting or erasing an entry to make the record look neat.
commonErrors.prevention: Strike through once, initial, date and give the reason for the correction.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Standard 3.2.2 covers cleanliness and the cleaning and sanitising of specific equipment (clauses 19 and 20, located from the Safe Food Australia contents). Check the current standard before relying on it.

The NSW Food Authority environmental swabbing guide (undated) says that swab and ATP results are read as trends, that sampling should wait for the sanitiser's contact time, and that contact plates and dipslides are not conclusive for specific pathogens. Its state is NSW, and it does not set release criteria.

Sanitiser and cleaning products are hazardous chemicals. The Safe Work Australia code on hazardous chemicals says the current safety data sheet for each chemical must be readily accessible to workers who use it, and that the register must be kept current (sections 1.6 and 2.2 read in the code).

Release of production, certification of sanitation and any statement of microbiological clearance are authorised decisions made by the responsible person under the site's food safety program. This lesson does not authorise release, sanitation certification or microbiological clearance, and completing it does not make a cleaner a tester, auditor or food safety officer.
The Safe Food Australia guide treats a food safety program as a written set of controls held at the premises (Standard 3.2.2, clause 1, pp. 15-16 as located in the guide).

qualityStandard: Each checklist line in the simulated sign-off is classed as cleaning, verification, monitoring or release, with the classification stated.
Every step not observed in the practical is marked not verified, with a reason and a named person to verify it.
The premature restart request in the case study is refused, recorded with the requester and time, and escalated.
No record in the exercise uses sterility, pathogen-free or allergen-free wording.
documentationEvidence: Annotated sign-off checklist showing observed, not verified and release lines separately.
Refusal and escalation record for the premature restart request, with time, requester and pending items.
Correction example showing a single strike-through, initials, date and reason.
summary: A cleaning checklist records cleaning work; it is not a test result and it is not a release.
Mark every step you did not see as not verified, and never carry a tick forward.
Refuse and escalate a premature restart, and keep the stop until the authorised person decides in writing.

knowledgeChecks.question: Does a completed cleaning checklist show that the line is free of micro-organisms?
options: Yes, it is the proof that the whole line is free of micro-organisms
Yes, if it is signed by a supervisor who checked the line at the end
No, verification, monitoring and release are separate records and decisions

knowledgeChecks.question: A step on the checklist was not seen. What should you do?
options: Mark it as not verified, with the reason
Tick it to keep the list moving along on time
Remove it from the list so it is not seen

knowledgeChecks.question: A supervisor asks you to sign for a restart while results are pending. What is correct?
options: Sign it, because the line looks ready for the restart now
Sign it and add a note saying the results are pending
Refuse, record the request, and escalate to the authorised person
